# Introduction

Innovation is widely regarded as a cornerstone of firm competitiveness. The resource-based view (RBV) establishes that R&D investments generate knowledge assets that are difficult to imitate, underpinning sustained competitive advantage [@barneyFirmResourcesSustained1991b. The absorptive capacity framework further argues that firms with higher R&D commitment develop a stronger ability to recognise, assimilate, and exploit external knowledge, amplifying the long-run performance benefits of innovation [@cohenAbsorptiveCapacityNew1990].

Yet this long-run optimism coexists with a striking short-run regularity: under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), most R&D outlays must be expensed immediately rather than capitalised, creating a mechanical reduction in current-period earnings. This tension is particularly acute for SMEs, which typically lack the financial slack available to large multinationals to absorb short-run earnings penalties [@fazzariFinancingConstraintsCorporate1988].

Prior empirical work documents significant heterogeneity in innovation-performance outcomes. @rosenbuschInnovationAlwaysBeneficial2011 show in a meta-analysis that the innovation-performance relationship is positive on average but highly context-dependent, while @hashiImpactInnovationActivities2013 find that the translation of innovation inputs into performance depends critically on firm capabilities and market conditions.

This research note addresses two gaps using a panel of European EUR-reporting SMEs from Compustat Global over 2015-2024. We provide within-firm causal estimates of the short-run R&D-performance relationship using two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimation [@mundlakPoolingTimeSeries1978], and examine whether firm size moderates this relationship.

> **Research question:** Does R&D intensity affect current-period firm performance among European SMEs, and does firm size moderate this relationship?

# Theoretical Background and Hypotheses

## R&D Intensity and Firm Performance

The RBV holds that competitive advantage derives from firm-specific resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable [@barneyFirmResourcesSustained1991b. R&D investment generates proprietary knowledge and intellectual property that cannot be costlessly replicated, translating into performance advantages through product differentiation and superior absorptive capacity [@cohenAbsorptiveCapacityNew1990].

However, the RBV argument pertains to the *long run*. In the short run, IFRS accounting requires R&D expenditures to be expensed in the period incurred, creating a mechanical wedge between accounting performance and underlying value creation. Every euro spent on R&D in year $t$ reduces reported RoA in year $t$, while commercial returns accrue only after a development and commercialisation lag.

For European SMEs, this dynamic is amplified by structural resource constraints. Unlike large multinationals, SMEs lack diversification and financial buffers that insulate performance from innovation expenditure [@fazzariFinancingConstraintsCorporate1988]. @rosenbuschInnovationAlwaysBeneficial2011 document that the innovation-performance link is weaker and more variable among smaller firms.

> **H1:** R&D intensity negatively affects current-period RoA among European SMEs, reflecting the immediate expensing effect under IFRS.
>
> *Test: β(rd_intensity) < 0 and statistically significant*

## The Moderating Role of Firm Size

The absorptive capacity framework [@cohenAbsorptiveCapacityNew1990] provides a basis for expecting firm size to moderate the R&D-performance relationship. Larger SMEs, with more extensive employee bases, greater functional expertise, and more financial slack, are better positioned to convert R&D inputs into commercialisable outputs. @hashiImpactInnovationActivities2013 provide supporting evidence that firm capabilities are a key boundary condition of the innovation-performance relationship.

> **H2:** Firm size positively moderates the R&D intensity-RoA relationship --- larger SMEs experience a smaller earnings penalty from R&D investment.
>
> *Test: β(rd_intensity × ln_at) > 0*

# Data and Method

## Sample

The empirical analysis draws on annual firm-level data from the WRDS Compustat Global database (`comp_global_daily.g_funda`). The sample is restricted to EUR-reporting firms satisfying the EU SME definition (fewer than 250 employees or total assets not exceeding €43 million) over fiscal years 2015-2024. We apply standard data quality filters and require at least three consecutive firm-year observations. The resulting unbalanced panel comprises `{python} f"{n_obs:,}"` firm-years from `{python} f"{n_firms:,}"` unique firms across 26 European countries.

## Variables

**Dependent variable.** Firm performance is operationalised as return on assets (RoA), calculated as net income divided by total assets (`nicon / at`).

**Independent variable.** R&D intensity is measured as R&D expenditure divided by total assets (`xrd / at`). Firms not disclosing R&D are assigned zero. Approximately `{python} f"{rd_share}"` % of firm-years report positive R&D expenditure.

**Moderator.** Firm size is the natural logarithm of total assets (`log(at)`), entering both as moderator and control variable.

**Control variables.** We include leverage (`dltt / at`), capital expenditure intensity (`capx / at`), and cash ratio (`che / at`). All continuous variables are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles [@wilcoxIntroductionRobustEstimation2012].

| Variable | Field(s) | Formula | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| RoA | `nicon`, `at` | `nicon / at` | Dependent (Y) |
| R&D intensity | `xrd`, `at` | `xrd.fillna(0) / at` | Independent (X) |
| R&D × Size | --- | `rd_intensity × ln_at` | H2 interaction |
| Firm size | `at` | `log(at)` | Moderator + Control |
| Leverage | `dltt`, `at` | `dltt / at` | Control |
| CAPX intensity | `capx`, `at` | `capx / at` | Control |
| Cash ratio | `che`, `at` | `che / at` | Control |

: Variable overview {#tbl-variables}

## Estimation Strategy

We estimate a two-way fixed effects (TWFE) panel model:

$$\text{RoA}_{it} = \beta_1 \text{R\&D}_{it} + \beta_2 (\text{R\&D} \times \text{Size})_{it} + \gamma X_{it} + \mu_i + \lambda_t + \epsilon_{it}$$

where $\mu_i$ are firm fixed effects and $\lambda_t$ are year fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the firm level following @petersenEstimatingStandardErrors2009. The preference for fixed over random effects is supported by a Hausman-type comparison [@mundlakPoolingTimeSeries1978]: the FE estimate (-0.534) diverges substantially from the RE estimate (-0.777), consistent with correlation between firm-level unobservables and R&D intensity.

The RoA distribution exhibits left-skew typical of SME panel data: the median of `{python} f"{panel['roa'].median():.3f}"` indicates marginal profitability, while the mean of `{python} f"{panel['roa'].mean():.3f}"` is pulled below by loss-making firms. R&D intensity has a median of zero --- only `{python} f"{rd_share}"` % of firm-years report positive R&D, consistent with the concentration of formal R&D investment among a minority of technologically active SMEs [@rosenbuschInnovationAlwaysBeneficial2011].

## Regression Results

```{python}
#| label: tbl-regression
#| tbl-cap: "Regression results. Dependent variable: RoA. Clustered SEs at firm level in Models (2)-(3). * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."
results[['(1) OLS', '(2) TWFE', '(3) TWFE+H2']]
```

**H1 --- R&D intensity and RoA.** R&D intensity enters with a negative and significant coefficient across all specifications. The TWFE estimate (Model 2) is $\hat{\beta}_1 =$ -0.534 (p < 0.01). **H1 is supported.** Expensing R&D under IFRS creates an immediate drag on profitability [@cohenAbsorptiveCapacityNew1990; @hashiImpactInnovationActivities2013].

The OLS coefficient (-0.784) exceeds the TWFE coefficient by 32% in absolute magnitude, consistent with omitted variable bias. Firm fixed effects eliminate this confound by exploiting only within-firm variation over time [@mundlakPoolingTimeSeries1978].

**H2 --- Firm size as moderator.** The interaction term (Model 3) is positive ($\hat{\beta}_2 =$ 0.060) but not significant (p = 0.425). **H2 is not supported**, though the direction is consistent with absorptive capacity theory [@cohenAbsorptiveCapacityNew1990].

# Discussion and Conclusion

## Discussion

The finding that R&D intensity negatively affects current-period RoA does not imply R&D destroys value. Rather, it reflects the temporal mismatch in IFRS accounting: SMEs bear the full accounting cost of R&D immediately, while accruing benefits across subsequent periods --- the necessary price of building durable knowledge assets [@barneyFirmResourcesSustained1991b @cohenAbsorptiveCapacityNew1990].

This has policy implications. If the short-run earnings penalty is visible to lenders and investors relying on accounting metrics, it may create a bias against R&D commitment among SMEs under profitability pressure [@fazzariFinancingConstraintsCorporate1988]. R&D tax credits or innovation subsidies may partially offset this deterrent.

## Conclusion

This research note examines the short-run effect of R&D intensity on firm performance among European SMEs using `{python} f"{n_obs:,}"` firm-years from `{python} f"{n_firms:,}"` firms across 26 countries over 2015-2024. H1 is strongly supported: higher R&D intensity is associated with significantly lower RoA ($\hat{\beta} =$ -0.534, p < 0.01), with the effect attenuated by 32% once firm fixed effects are controlled. H2 is not supported at conventional significance levels.

Three limitations apply: measurement error from zero-imputation of non-disclosing firms; the 10-year window may not span the full R&D payoff cycle; and Compustat coverage skews toward listed firms, limiting generalisation to private SMEs.
